newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Orders rise shows German recovery on track.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Orders rise shows German recovery on track.

text.p: German industry orders in March rose by 1.1 percent compared to the previous month, helped by a big rise in orders for goods manufactured in the formerly communist east, the Economics Ministry said on Tuesday.

Analysts welcomed the data, and said it pointed to a healthy rise in gross domestic product in the first quarter of this year after two quarters of stagnation. Economic growth is likely to gather pace during the second quarter, they added.

"The orders data were much stronger than expected and they confirm that the economy is growing faster than generally expected, particularly in the industrial sector," said Joachim Fels, economist at Morgan Stanley in Frankfurt.

Industrial orders, calculated using Bundesbank historical data, were up 5.5 percent in March compared to the same month a year earlier. The figures are provisional, seasonally-adjusted and expressed in volume terms.
In western Germany, orders were up by 0.7 percent compared to February and rose by 4.7 percent year-on-year.
In the east, orders surged by 7.4 percent and were up a whopping 23.2 percent compared to March 1996.
A Reuters survey of economists had shown that they had expected March industrial orders to be little changed against the previous month.

The Economics Ministry said the orders data was boosted by a series of large contracts, which helped foreign orders show a two percent gain in March while orders from within Germany were up by just 0.7 percent.
Uwe Angenendt at BHF-Bank also said the orders data were stronger than expected.
"It now looks as if for the first quarter of 1997 orders will be up 1.5 percent from the previous quarter," he said.
"That is fairly positive and we think gross domestic product for the first quarter will definitely be up 0.5 percent from the previous quarter, possibly even more."

Fels said: "We're seeing strong demand from within Germany, especially for investment goods and we're seeing that the domestic investment cycle is beginning to pick up. But domestic demand for consumer goods remains weak."
"I see first quarter GDP rising by 0.7 or 0.8 percent from the previous quarter and there will be a clear acceleration in the second quarter, with growth likely to be about one percent.
Fels is forecasting growth of three percent this year, which is above the government's own forecast of 2.5 percent.
Taken together with April unemployment data, which showed a modest rise in seasonally-adjusted joblessness, some economists said the economic picture was still mixed.
"The economy is gaining, step-by-step, although it is hard going," said Peter Pietsch, economist at Commerzbank.
The orders data, a leading indicator, will not feed through into an early fall in joblessness after seasonally-adjusted data earlier showed a small rise for April, Pietsch said.
Adjusted unemployment rose in April by 8,000 to 4.299 million, while the politically-significant headline figure fell by 130,000.
"We expect unemployment, a lagging indicator, to fall in the second half of the year," Pietsch added.
Pietsch, representing a minority view among economists, said that stubbornly high unemployment would not hamper efforts to cut government borrowing to qualify this year for Europe's single currency.

He said that Finance Minister Theo Waigel would only need to make spending cuts -- and not raise taxes -- to get the budget deficit down to the target of three percent of GDP stipulated by the Maastricht treaty.

"I am still very optimistic that Germany can achieve the deficit criterion," he said. "In the second half of the year the federal government and the states should be able to put together the necessary savings."
